extracted.intended_audience: students, researchers, and practitioners of crisis communication / public relations
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes Benoit's image restoration (image repair) theory: conditions, assumptions, factors, and a typology of strategies organizations or individuals can use to respond to reputation-damaging events. Useful for analyzing or planning crisis-response messaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two components of an attack
rubrics_metrics.description: Two components must be present in a given attack to the image of an individual or organization: The accused is held responsible for an action; the act is considered offensive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the necessary conditions for image restoration strategies to be relevant — if either component is missing, an image-restoration response may not be required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumption: Communication is a goal-directed activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Communicators may have multiple goals that are not collectively compatible, but people try to achieve goals that are most important to them at the time, with reasonable cost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose response strategies that align with the actor's prioritized goals and consider trade-offs between competing goals when planning messages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumption: Maintaining a favorable reputation is a key goal of communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Because face, image, or reputation is valued as important, individuals or organizations are motivated to take action when it is compromised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat reputation protection as a central objective when selecting and framing crisis responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception is fundamental to image restoration
rubrics_metrics.description: The accused actor will not engage in a defensive strategy unless the perception exists that he is at fault.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategy choice depends on perceived fault; account for factors such as credibility, audience perceptions, and the degree of offensiveness when deciding whether and how to respond.

rubrics_metrics.name: Image repair factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Some image repair factors include: Crisis responsibility (how much a company or person is responsible), Crisis type (what type of crisis is happening), Organizational reputation (the known reputation and behavior of a company or a person).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess these factors to predict audience reaction and to tailor appropriate strategies (e.g., greater responsibility calls for stronger remedial responses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Denial
rubrics_metrics.description: The accused may simply deny that the act occurred, or shift the blame to the 'real' culprit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Denial is appropriate when the actor is innocent or can credibly attribute the act to another party; risks include credibility loss if evidence contradicts denial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evading responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: When unable to deny performing the act, the accused may attempt to evade responsibility. This strategy has four components: provocation, defeasibility, unaccountability, bona fide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Components explained: Provocation — claim the act was a response to another wrongful act; Defeasibility — plead lack of knowledge or control; Unaccountability — excuse factors beyond control; Bona fide — ask not to be held fully responsible based on good motives. Use these to explain or mitigate perceived responsibility, but audience credibility and evidence matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reducing offensiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: The accused may attempt to reduce the degree of negative feeling experienced by the audience. This strategy has six components: bolstering, minimization, differentiation, transcendence, ad hominem, compensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Components explained: Bolstering — remind audience of prior good acts; Minimization — convince audience the act is less serious; Differentiation — distinguish the act from more offensive acts; Transcendence — place act in a broader, less offensive frame; Ad hominem — attack accusers or their credibility; Compensation — offer to redress victims. These tactics aim to lessen negative sentiment but can backfire if perceived as dismissive or evasive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrective action
rubrics_metrics.description: The accused claims that they will correct the problem, which can involve restoring the situation to its prior state, or promising to make changes to prevent its reoccurrence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promising and taking concrete corrective steps helps repair reputation; effectiveness increases when actions are specific, visible, and publicized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mortification
rubrics_metrics.description: The accused admits responsibility and asks for forgiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mortification (full apology/acceptance of responsibility) is often recommended when guilt is clear; it should be sincere and accompanied by corrective action where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benoit's prescriptive recommendations from case studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Based on Benoit's case studies: the dominant recommendation is for an organization to immediately admit fault/accept responsibility; corrective actions should be taken and publicized; bolstering is directly related to the charge and is often effective; if the organization is innocent, denial is effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summary guidance: prefer mortification + corrective action when guilty, publicize remedial actions, use bolstering to reinforce positive aspects, and use denial only when innocence is credible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations and cautions (Coombs critique)
rubrics_metrics.description: Coombs argues that situational crisis communication theory found no support for always using mortification and corrective action; in some crises (e.g., criminal violation like racial discrimination) mortification and corrective action had no greater effect than bolstering. He recommends examining many similar crises to identify patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat Benoit's prescriptions as universally optimal — consider crisis type, context, and empirical evidence from comparable cases before adopting a response strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication/campaign recommendations from Cola Wars analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: From analysis of Coke/Pepsi ads: companies should avoid making false claims, provide adequate support for claims, develop themes throughout a campaign, and avoid arguments that might backfire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When mounting a defensive or competitive campaign, ensure factual accuracy, substantiation, consistent thematic messaging, and assess risk of backlash.
